text: We've built subscriptions, and we've picked delivery extensions. The last piece is telling a subscription when to actually run — and Reporting Services gives you two genuinely different ways to do that.

Right in the New Subscription page's Schedule section, you get the choice. Shared schedule hands you a dropdown of schedules someone's already created. Report-specific schedule is selected here instead, with Edit schedule next to it — and underneath, a preview of what it's currently set to: 2 AM every day, starting October 1st, 2020.

Click Edit schedule and this is what opens — the same recurrence picker whether you're defining a report-specific schedule or creating a brand-new shared one. Hour, Day, Week, Month, or Once, then the specifics underneath: which days, what time, when it starts and optionally ends. Both schedule types are built from exactly this same picker — the only difference is where the result gets stored afterward.

If ten subscriptions all need to run at 6 AM after a nightly load finishes, a shared schedule means "6 AM" lives in exactly one place — move the load to 6:30, and you edit one schedule instead of ten. Shared schedules can also be paused and resumed, which a report-specific schedule simply can't do. Delete a shared schedule that's in use, though, and Reporting Services doesn't orphan anything — it creates an individual report-specific schedule for every subscription that used it, copying the same timing over first, so nothing silently stops running.

None of this runs itself — it's backed by real infrastructure. Creating a schedule writes its recurrence information to the report server database and creates a corresponding SQL Server Agent job. This is what that actually looks like in Management Studio: one job per schedule, each one named with an unreadable GUID instead of a report name, because a single schedule can back more than one subscription at once.

When that job fires, it drops an event into a queue the Scheduling and Delivery Processor polls — every 10 seconds, by default. The processor picks the event up, calls the report processor to run the report, and hands the result to whichever delivery extension the subscription specifies. Stop SQL Server Agent for a stretch of time, and every scheduled operation that should have fired during that window is simply lost — it isn't queued up to catch up later.
That's Chapter 7 — subscriptions built, delivery extensions chosen, schedules understood. Next up, Chapter 8: Deployment and Administration, starting with Report Server administration itself.
